title: Carbonyl addition
goal: How nucleophiles add to C=O, and what the tetrahedral intermediate does next.

problemSets.title: Nucleophilic addition
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: A nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon; the π electrons move onto oxygen.
problemSets.conceptCard:
The C=O bond is polarised: carbon is **electron-poor**, oxygen **electron-rich**. Every addition is the same two arrows:

1. the nucleophile's electrons form a bond to the **carbonyl carbon**
2. the **C=O π pair** moves onto oxygen

The alkoxide formed is a base: a proton source (the solvent, HCN, or an *acid work-up*) turns it into the alcohol. Hydride from **B–H** and carbon from **C–Mg** count as nucleophiles too.

setItems.whyThisOne: Hydride from a B–H bond; methanol supplies the proton.
A new C–C bond; the acid comes only at the end.
HCN protonates the alkoxide and gives back cyanide.

problemSets.title: Hydrates, hemiacetals and acetals
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Water and alcohols add reversibly; acid lets the OH leave and a second alcohol add.
problemSets.conceptCard:
Water and alcohols are **weak nucleophiles**. A catalyst helps:

- **base** makes a better nucleophile (HO⁻ instead of H₂O)
- **acid** makes a better electrophile (the protonated carbonyl)

In acid a hemiacetal goes further. Protonating its OH makes **water a leaving group**, the OR lone pair pushes it out, and the **oxocarbenium ion** takes a second alcohol: an *acetal*. Every proton comes from a real acid and goes to a real base.

setItems.whyThisOne: Base catalysis: hydroxide adds, water gives the proton.
Acid catalysis, and a six-membered ring closes.
The full sequence through the oxocarbenium ion.

problemSets.title: Imines and enamines
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Amines add, water leaves, and the iminium ion loses a proton from N or from C.
problemSets.conceptCard:
An amine adds like an alcohol, and the hemiaminal loses water the same way: protonate the OH, then the **nitrogen lone pair** pushes water out to give an **iminium ion**.

- A **primary amine** leaves an N–H on the iminium ion: losing it gives an *imine*.
- A **secondary amine** has no N–H left, so a C–H next to C=N⁺ is lost: an *enamine*.

A mild hydride donor reduces the iminium ion to an amine: *reductive amination*.

setItems.whyThisOne: Every proton transfer of imine formation, at pH 4–5.
No N–H left: the proton comes off carbon.
NaBH₃CN reduces the iminium ion, not the ketone.

problemSets.title: Ylides
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: A carbanion next to P⁺ adds to C=O, and the strong P=O bond drives off the alkene.
problemSets.conceptCard: A strong base removes a proton from the carbon next to a **phosphonium** ion: the **ylide** has C⁻ beside P⁺. Its carbon adds to the carbonyl carbon like any carbon nucleophile, but the oxygen then bonds to phosphorus. The four-membered ring falls apart to an **alkene** and Ph₃P=O: the *Wittig reaction* swaps C=O for C=C.

setItems.whyThisOne: Butyllithium as a base: making the ylide.
C=O becomes C=C through the oxaphosphetane.

problemSets.title: Checkpoint
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Add to C=O, move the protons, and decide what leaves.
problemSets.conceptCard: Reactions from every set, shuffled, names hidden until you finish. Three attempts per step.

setItems.whyThisOne: A carbon nucleophile and a work-up.
Proton transfers and loss of water.
